forces.name: Rivalry among existing competitors
forces.short: Aggressive pricing by supermarkets and minimarkets pressures MPPA’s sales.
forces.theory: Assess the number of rivals, differentiation, switching costs and pressure to compete on price or service.
evidence: MPPA’s 2020 report identifies aggressive price competition from expanding supermarkets and minimarkets as a factor affecting its performance.
forces.reading: Hypermart was much smaller by sales than Indomaret and Alfamart in the case’s 2020 comparison. App-based ordering added competition on convenience.
forces.salesLink: MPPA needs to win profitable grocery purchases through competitive prices, accessible stores and convenient ordering.
forces.limit: Exhibit 8 compares selected retail chains, not the entire market or online-only sales. Hypermart is a brand, not total MPPA. HappyFresh platform orders can overlap partner-retailer sales; downloads, traffic, funding and GMV cannot be treated as comparable revenue. No causal share of MPPA’s sales decline is established. LotteMart’s separate-company financial-statement revenue is added to the case estimates on a common rupiah scale using 2020 average exchange rates; currency conversion does not reconcile differences in reporting scope.
forces.industryContext: Large grocery chains and app-based services compete for household grocery spending.

forces.name: Bargaining power of buyers
forces.short: Shoppers’ ability to switch stores constrains MPPA’s pricing.
forces.theory: Buyer power depends on purchase concentration, switching costs, product differentiation and price sensitivity.
evidence: No individual customer accounted for more than 10% of MPPA’s 2020 net sales.
MPPA regularly compared market prices across fresh food, groceries and household essentials to retain customers.
forces.reading: Individual shoppers have little negotiating leverage, but can easily redirect their next purchase. MPPA competes on price and convenience to retain them.
forces.salesLink: MPPA’s sales depend on retaining frequent purchases across many customers.
forces.limit: MPPA’s pricing actions demonstrate pressure to retain customers. The report does not quantify a customer-switching rate or the sales recovered through price matching.
forces.industryContext: Discounts, nearby stores and delivery give grocery shoppers several purchasing options.

forces.name: Threat of new entrants
forces.short: MPPA’s logistics network raises the cost of entry at national scale.
forces.theory: Assess entry barriers such as scale, capital, brand recognition and access to supply and distribution.
evidence: MPPA’s 2020 report identifies its logistics network as a barrier to new retail entrants.
forces.reading: MPPA’s established logistics raises the cost of replicating its national network. Smaller operators can still enter individual neighbourhoods.
forces.salesLink: MPPA has protection at network scale, while local stores compete within each shopping area.
forces.limit: The logistics advantage is MPPA management’s stated assessment, supported by its disclosed infrastructure. It is not a guarantee against entry or proof that every new outlet took MPPA sales.
forces.industryContext: Reliable sourcing, suitable locations and distribution capacity create barriers to establishing a grocery chain.

forces.name: Threat of substitutes
forces.short: Early-2020 meal habits continued to support grocery purchases.
forces.theory: A substitute meets the same underlying need in a different way; assess its relative price, performance and switching costs.
forces.reading: Home cooking remained important in early 2020. The survey indicates continued demand for cooking ingredients.
forces.salesLink: MPPA competed for household grocery spending across physical and online channels.
forces.limit: Nielsen’s consumer-study fieldwork was 7–10 March 2020. The findings describe that period, not a full-year change in MPPA sales.
forces.industryContext: Restaurant meals are an alternative to buying ingredients for home cooking.

forces.name: Bargaining power of suppliers
forces.short: A dispersed supplier base and formal procurement support MPPA’s negotiating position.
forces.theory: Assess supplier concentration, unique inputs, switching costs and the importance of the retailer to suppliers.
evidence: No single supplier’s inventory purchases exceeded 10% of MPPA’s net sales in 2020.
MPPA used formal vendor selection and agreed trading terms, alongside local purchasing and SME supplier development.
forces.reading: MPPA’s supplier base and formal procurement processes support its negotiating position. Local purchasing broadens its sourcing relationships.
forces.salesLink: Supplier terms affect merchandise margins; product availability affects completed customer purchases.
forces.limit: The 10% denominator is net sales, not purchases. MPPA’s processes do not by themselves prove better terms, easy replacement of every brand, or an absence of supply disruption.
forces.industryContext: Retailers faced distribution and stock-allocation risks in early 2020.

ratingBasis.rivalry: High: active price/service competition and incumbent expansion.
ratingBasis.buyers: Moderate: easy retailer choice versus fragmented buying and limited individual negotiation.
ratingBasis.entrants: Moderate overall pressure: MPPA’s three-DC logistics network and its stated role as an entry barrier; independent chains must build or access distribution while small local operators require less geographic coverage.
ratingBasis.substitutes: Limited restaurant-meal substitution pressure in the early-2020 period covered by Nielsen’s survey. Home preparation remains relevant to grocery demand; analysis then examines where and how households shop. No KFC outlet counts or MPPA fresh-food share used to infer this force.
ratingBasis.suppliers: Low–moderate for MPPA merchandise sourcing: its own supplier-concentration disclosure, procurement/trading processes and local SME supplier development. Competitor sourcing policies are not evidence of MPPA capability.
